sample_values: {'datasets_used': 'Cross-sectional survey data from 937 medical students at Anhui Medical University, China; validated self-administered questionnaire based on prior AI attitude scales/TAME-ChatGPT tool; demographic and DeepSeek usage/attitude responses collected in July 2025.', 'methods': 'Cross-sectional stratified cluster random sampling survey; validated self-administered Likert-scale questionnaire with screening questions, cognition/attitude scale (13 items) and usage pattern scale (25 items); confirmatory factor analysis, pilot testing, descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis H tests, and multiple linear regression to identify predictors of usage experience and attitudes.', 'key_findings': 'Most medical students were aware of DeepSeek (93.3%) and had used it (81.6%); 94.8% would be willing to use and recommend it and 90.2% would use it to help complete tasks. Students saw benefits such as saving time and aiding research, but many were concerned about information reliability, plagiarism, overreliance, privacy, and reduced critical thinking. Usage experience and attitudes varied by gender, educational level, major, and research field.', 'evaluation_metrics': "Cronbach's alpha (0.83); confirmatory factor analysis fit indices (χ2/df, RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, TLI); mean scores; median (interquartile range); Mann-Whitney U test; Kruskal-Wallis H test; multiple linear regression coefficients (β), 95% confidence intervals, p-values; R2 and adjusted R2.", 'biomedical_task': "Surveying medical students' attitudes, usage patterns, and factors associated with adoption of DeepSeek in medical education.", 'llm_model_or_family': 'DeepSeek large language model', 'biomedical_domain_context': "Medical education in China; medical students' use of generative AI for learning, coursework, and research.", 'study_type': 'Cross-sectional survey study', 'comparison_baselines': "Compared usage experience and attitudes across demographic groups (male vs female, undergraduate vs master's degree, different majors and research fields); questionnaire scale adapted from TAME-ChatGPT/previous AI attitude scales rather than a direct model-performance baseline.", 'limitations_or_risks': 'Self-reported questionnaire data may be affected by reporting and recall bias; single-university sample with many undergraduates limits generalizability; scale was adapted from ChatGPT without full re-validation for DeepSeek, introducing possible measurement bias; residual confounding from prior AI training or institutional exposure; concerns about information accuracy, plagiarism, privacy security, overreliance, and reduced critical thinking.'}

{'datasets_used': 'Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) term–identifier mappings (800 sampled facts); Gene Ontology (GO) term–identifier mappings (802 sampled facts, split into 401 trained and 401 withheld/untrained facts); PubMed Central (PMC) full-text records for term and identifier frequency counts; HPO phenotype.hpoa annotation file; GO goa_human.gaf annotation file', 'methods': 'Llama-3.1-8B Instruct was fine-tuned with parameter-efficient LoRA (rank 64, scaling alpha 128) on ontology term-to-identifier mapping tasks using five paraphrased instruction templates per fact. Fact acquisition and fact loss were reframed as discrete epoch-indexed time-to-event outcomes. Baseline latent knowledge was probed with repeated stochastic decoding (50 samples per fact) before fine-tuning. Deterministic greedy decoding was used to assess exact identifier retrieval after each epoch. Kaplan–Meier estimators were used for acquisition/loss curves, and Cox proportional hazards models were used to test predictors such as latent knowledge and corpus-based fact support. A discrete-time logistic regression sensitivity analysis was also performed for HPO trained-fact acquisition.', 'key_findings': 'Baseline retrieval was low (1.1% for HPO and 5.5% for GO). After 20 epochs, retrieval rose to 71.9% for trained HPO facts, 61.8% for trained GO facts, and 11.2% for untrained GO facts. Latent-knowledge-positive facts were acquired faster and more completely than latent-knowledge-negative facts. Corpus-based support also helped: HPO annotation frequency and HPO identifier frequency in PMC predicted trained-fact acquisition, and GO identifier frequency in PMC predicted untrained-fact acquisition. Untrained-fact acquisition was uncommon overall (5.8% of baseline-incorrect withheld GO facts). Fact loss was substantial among GO facts correct at baseline (54.5%), and was more frequent among withheld than trained facts. The study concludes that pretraining-derived latent structure and continued training exposure both influence the efficiency and stability of biomedical fact learning during fine-tuning.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Deterministic accuracy / exact identifier match; stochastic support score (fraction of 50 stochastic samples producing the correct identifier); Kaplan–Meier survival estimates and cumulative acquisition/retention curves; Cox proportional hazards hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals; log-rank (Mantel–Cox) tests; concordance for the untrained-fact Cox model; Schoenfeld residual tests for proportional hazards; discrete-time odds ratios in sensitivity analysis', 'biomedical_task': 'Biomedical ontology term normalization / term-to-identifier mapping; fact acquisition and retention during fine-tuning of biomedical ontology knowledge', 'llm_model_or_family': 'Llama-3.1-8B Instruct', 'biomedical_domain_context': 'Biomedical ontologies and terminology normalization in biomedicine, specifically the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) and Gene Ontology (GO); broader implications for biomedical informatics and clinical terminology retrieval', 'study_type': 'Original research; methodological proof-of-concept benchmark evaluation using survival analysis', 'comparison_baselines': 'Baseline pre-fine-tuning model performance at epoch 0; comparison between latent-knowledge-positive and latent-knowledge-negative facts; comparison between trained and untrained GO facts; univariate comparisons for fact loss between facts with and without loss', 'limitations_or_risks': 'The study was limited to HPO and GO term–identifier mappings and may not generalize to other factual acquisition tasks or ontology systems. It used one model family and a fixed LoRA configuration without broad hyperparameter exploration. Analyses were epoch-indexed rather than continuous-time. Fact loss analysis was exploratory because few baseline-correct facts were available. The work did not examine internal mechanisms such as logits or representation changes. Approximately 40% of HPO terms and 54% of GO terms lacking curated annotations were excluded, so results may overestimate performance relative to the full ontologies. The model was evaluated without retrieval augmentation or external tools. Repeated stochastic decoding is computationally demanding, and fine-tuning can also cause fact loss/forgetting of previously correct mappings.'}

{'datasets_used': '11 expert-formulated medical physics questions related to oncology radiotherapy, including breast carcinoma, head and neck cancer, cervical cancer, brain metastasis, and lung carcinoma; responses were evaluated against internationally recognized guidelines and standards (ESTRO, AAPM TG-218, TG-142, TG-119, ICRU Reports 83, 62, and 50).', 'methods': 'Comparative benchmark evaluation of three AI chatbots (ChatGPT 5.2, DeepSeek V 3.2, Gemini 3.0) using 11 domain-specific prompts prepared by clinical medical physicists; each question was asked once per chatbot on a predetermined date, responses were copied into Word, and three expert medical physicists independently scored them for correctness, completeness, readability, irrelevant data, real-world applicability in the Indian scenario, reliability, and repeatability; statistical analysis used one-way ANOVA, ICC, and kappa.', 'key_findings': 'DeepSeek achieved the highest mean correctness and the most complete responses overall, while ChatGPT was comparatively easier to read; Gemini generally performed worse on correctness and generated more irrelevant data. None of the chatbots were sufficiently capable of replicating human intelligence across correctness, completeness, real-world applicability, and language ease, so they should be used as adjuncts rather than replacements for medical professionals.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Correctness, completeness, language/readability (Flesch-Kincaid reading ease), irrelevant data, additional relevant data, real-world applicability in the Indian scenario, grade of reliability, repeatability of responses, ANOVA, ICC, and kappa coefficient.', 'biomedical_task': 'Answering domain-specific medical physics questions in oncology radiotherapy, including treatment planning, dose prescription, motion management, adaptive replanning, and quality assurance.', 'llm_model_or_family': 'ChatGPT 5.2, DeepSeek V 3.2, Gemini 3.0', 'biomedical_domain_context': 'Medical physics in oncology, especially radiotherapy for breast cancer, head and neck cancer, cervical cancer, lung cancer, and brain metastases; radiotherapy planning and quality assurance.', 'study_type': 'Comparative benchmark evaluation / expert-rated original research study', 'comparison_baselines': 'Compared among ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini; expert judgments were aligned with ESTRO, AAPM, and ICRU standards rather than a separate algorithmic baseline.', 'limitations_or_risks': 'None of the chatbots were good enough to replace human expertise; issues included incomplete answers, irrelevant or additional irrelevant data, variable repeatability, slower responses for some queries, and concerns about hallucination, privacy, data security, transparency, and regulatory/ethical risks.'}

{'datasets_used': 'Electronic health records from a single academic medical center; unstructured ophthalmology outpatient clinical notes from Byers Eye Institute at Stanford; STAnford Research Repository (STARR) query of patients with ICD-10 ischemic optic neuropathy codes (H47.01, H47.011, H47.012, H47.013, H47.019); expert neuro-ophthalmologist chart review labels used as reference standard.', 'methods': 'Retrospective cross-sectional study using locally deployed, privacy-preserving LLMs on anonymized longitudinal ophthalmology notes. Five models (Mistral Small 3.1, Magistral Small, Gemma3, MedGemma, GPT-OSS 20B) were evaluated with four approaches: basic prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using LangChain and Chroma vector database, 2-step agentic workflow, and 3-step agentic workflow. Ten percent of subjects were used for prompt refinement. Outputs were constrained to Yes/No in <answer> tags and compared against expert chart review. The best-performing model/approach was also used for feature-based classification (APD, optic disc edema, sudden onset).', 'key_findings': 'LLM approaches outperformed ICD-10 code-based case identification for acute NAION. Across approaches, PPV and accuracy were substantially higher than using ICD codes alone, and the Mistral Small 3.1 3-step agentic approach performed best overall (39 cases identified, PPV 0.85, accuracy 0.82, F1 0.75). False positives were mostly historical/chronic NAION rather than non-NAION diagnoses. The study concludes that local agentic LLMs can support scalable, privacy-preserving retrospective case identification from unstructured EHRs.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, F1 score; true positive/false positive/true negative/false negative counts; distribution of classifications.', 'biomedical_task': 'Retrospective chart review and case identification/classification of incident acute nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) from longitudinal ophthalmology electronic health records.', 'llm_model_or_family': 'Mistral Small 3.1 24B; Magistral Small 2509; Gemma3 27B; MedGemma 27B; GPT-OSS 20B.', 'biomedical_domain_context': 'Neuro-ophthalmology / ophthalmology; electronic health records; retrospective research on optic neuropathy case identification.', 'study_type': 'Retrospective cross-sectional benchmark evaluation of local LLM workflows against expert chart review.', 'comparison_baselines': 'ICD-10 code-based identification using 1, ≥2, and ≥3 ischemic optic neuropathy codes; expert neuro-ophthalmologist chart review as gold standard.', 'limitations_or_risks': 'Single-center retrospective data may limit generalizability; additional validation is needed in other cohorts and settings. No model identified all acute NAION cases. Performance tradeoffs existed between PPV and NPV. Smaller local models were not interchangeable and may perform worse on complex reasoning. RAG may fragment temporal/contextual information. Manual clinical expertise is still required for validation/adjudication.'}

{'datasets_used': '55 realistic synthetic pediatric clinical scenarios created by an experienced pediatrician; American Emergency Severity Index (ESI); Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS)', 'methods': 'Skyer benchmark evaluation of 15 LLMs using parent-description prompts for pediatric emergency department triage; each case was scored by models and by human experts; triage levels 4 and 5 were merged into a low-acuity group; a weighting system penalized over-triage and under-triage based on patient outcome, safety, satisfaction, resource use, staff fatigue, and ED flow; models were tested three times for consistency; Welch’s one-sided t-test, Mann–Whitney U test, Cohen’s D, and ICC were used in analysis', 'key_findings': 'ChatGPT-4.5-preview and Gemini-2.5_05-06 were the only models that significantly outperformed human triage experts and showed acceptable consistency; ChatGPT-4.5-preview achieved 77% accuracy and Gemini-2.5_05-06 achieved 74% accuracy; both had higher weighted scores than human experts and other models; the benchmark suggests these models can assist ED triage but should not replace human experts', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Accuracy, weighted triage score, over-triage rate, under-triage rate, consistency percentage, Welch’s one-sided t-test p-value, Cohen’s D effect size, Mann–Whitney U test, intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)', 'biomedical_task': 'Emergency department triage for pediatric patients', 'llm_model_or_family': 'ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-4.5-preview, Gemini-1.5-pro, Gemini-2.0-Pro experimental, Gemini-2.5_03-25, Gemini-2.5_05-06, DeepSeek-R1-7B, DeepSeek-R1-70B, Qwen-2.5, Phi-4-14B, Llama-3.3, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-27b-it, Gemma-3-12b-it, Gemma-3-27b-it', 'biomedical_domain_context': 'Pediatric emergency medicine and overcrowded emergency department triage', 'study_type': 'Benchmark evaluation study', 'comparison_baselines': 'Three experienced triage nurses and one physician (human triage experts); comparison across 15 LLMs', 'limitations_or_risks': 'Reliance on LLMs for triage raises ethical concerns; risk of hallucinations and unreliable non-expert patient interactions; overreliance could reduce professional medical care seeking; models are not suitable as replacements for human experts; synthetic scenarios may not fully capture real-world complexity'}

{'datasets_used': 'LMOD+ benchmark dataset (32,633 instances) curated from 10 publicly available ophthalmology datasets spanning five imaging modalities: Cataract-1K, OIMHS, Harvard FairSeg, CAU001, Cataract Detection 2, REFUGE, IDRiD, ORIGA, G1020, and BRSET. Balanced evaluation subsets were also used, including OIMHS, ICDR, SDRG, ORIGA, and BRSET-derived subsets.', 'methods': 'Unified data curation pipeline repurposing existing ophthalmology datasets into MLLM-compatible prompt-response tasks. Zero-shot evaluation of 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs across anatomical recognition, binary and multi-class disease diagnosis, disease staging, and demographic prediction. Additional experiments included stochastic sampling seed stability analysis, few-shot (3-shot) prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and self-consistency prompting. Supervised baselines were also trained: a CNN for anatomical recognition and RETFound fine-tuning for glaucoma and macular hole staging.', 'key_findings': 'Current general-domain and medical-domain MLLMs performed suboptimally on ophthalmic tasks. Best zero-shot results were Qwen-7B and InternVL models for disease screening (about 58%), but performance on disease staging and anatomical recognition remained low and often near random. InternVL-1.5-4B was competitive for anatomical recognition, and GPT-4o achieved the best overall anatomical recognition performance. Medical MLLMs such as LLaVA-Med and Med-Flamingo did not outperform general models. Supervised CNN baselines achieved much higher accuracies, indicating the benchmark is learnable and that domain-specific training is likely necessary. Demographic prediction was near chance, suggesting no strong detectable demographic bias under the tested setting.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Precision, recall, F1 score, hallucination resistance (HR), binary accuracy, multi-class accuracy, overall accuracy, sex accuracy, age accuracy; for subgroup analysis, accuracy and F1-score with 95% confidence intervals and chi-square test p-values.', 'biomedical_task': 'Ophthalmic multimodal benchmark evaluation for anatomical structure recognition, binary disease diagnosis, multi-class disease diagnosis, disease staging assessment, and demographic prediction from ophthalmic images.', 'llm_model_or_family': 'GPT-4o, LLaVA-Med, Med-Flamingo, Yi-VL, Qwen-VL-Chat, Qwen-3B, Qwen-7B, InternVL-1.5/2.0/2.5 series including MPO variants, DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny, DeepSeek-VL2-Small, LLaVA series.', 'biomedical_domain_context': 'Ophthalmology; retinal and eye disease imaging across color fundus photography, OCT, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy, lens photography, and surgical scenes.', 'study_type': 'Benchmark dataset and evaluation study; methodological paper with comparative benchmark evaluation and additional baseline training/ablation analyses.', 'comparison_baselines': 'Random baseline; supervised CNN baseline for anatomical recognition; RETFound fine-tuned for glaucoma and macular hole staging; comparisons across 24 MLLMs including general-purpose and medical-specific models.', 'limitations_or_risks': 'Overall MLLM performance was suboptimal and often near random on challenging ophthalmic tasks, especially staging and anatomical recognition. Models showed hallucinations, inconsistent reasoning, misinterpreted visual features, absent visual processing, and text generation failures. Few-shot, CoT, and self-consistency prompting sometimes improved recall but reduced format compliance and hallucination resistance. The study notes limited coverage of tasks beyond diagnosis/staging and that current zero-shot settings are particularly difficult.'}

{'datasets_used': '', 'methods': 'ChatGPT-generated assessment and plan notes were evaluated for outpatient gynecologic oncology encounters; the study focused on prompt elements associated with output accuracy and on provider assessment of the generated documentation. The abstract indicates a prompt-engineering approach tailored to subspecialty clinical context and established treatment standards.', 'key_findings': 'The paper reports that specific prompt engineering reflecting the gynecologic oncology context and established treatment standards may improve the consistency and reliability of AI-generated documentation. {'datasets_used': 'Large federated, de-identified US EHR platform spanning over 29 million patients; physician-adjudicated extracted-event reference standard for evaluation.', 'methods': 'Evidence-linked large language model (LLM) pipeline curated clinical notes to detect GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation, persistence, and compounding beyond structured prescription records; evaluated against an independent physician-adjudicated reference standard.', 'key_findings': 'The note-based LLM curation distinguished prescription intent from verified exposure and produced materially different initiation/persistence estimates than structured records. It identified documented initiation in 141,189 semaglutide patients and 62,040 tirzepatide patients, with note-confirmed 18-month persistence of 42.3% and 43.1%, respectively, versus higher structured-record estimates of 55.4% and 58.3%. Compounded exposure was detected in 1,696 frictionless initiators, and insurance/cost barriers, perioperative holds, and gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common documented reasons for discontinuation/barriers.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Accuracy for structural chunk triage (98.4%) and medication-status adjudication (88.2%); log-rank P < .001 for persistence trajectory differences; counts/percentages for initiation, persistence, and compounding ascertainment.', 'biomedical_task': 'Information extraction and evidence-linked curation of clinical notes for GLP-1 receptor agonist initiation, persistence, and compounding exposure ascertainment.', 'llm_model_or_family': 'An evidence-linked large language model (specific model name not stated in the provided abstract).', 'biomedical_domain_context': 'Electronic health records; real-world exposure ascertainment for incretin-based therapies / GLP-1 receptor agonists in obesity and diabetes care.', 'study_type': 'Methodological clinical validation study using an LLM pipeline on EHR data.', 'comparison_baselines': 'Structured prescription-record ascertainment; independent physician-adjudicated extracted-event reference standard.', 'limitations_or_risks': 'Structured prescription records may capture prescribing intent rather than confirmed use; potential time-to-market confounding was noted; note-based ascertainment depends on clinical documentation quality and availability.', 'source_urls': ['https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42433615/'], 'confidence': 'medium'}

{'datasets_used': 'MIMIC-III; University of Washington Medical Center (UWMC) EHR notes; Boston Children’s Hospital (BCH) notes; general-domain corpora cited for comparison including Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, The Pile, and RefinedWeb; LLaMA tokenizer applied to medical notes from MIMIC-III, UWMC, and BCH', 'methods': 'Analytical/methodological paper using scaling-law-based estimates to relate model size, token count, dataset size, compute cost, and training budget for LLMs trained on EHR data; tokenization of EHR notes with the LLaMA tokenizer to estimate tokens per gigabyte; comparison of two training scenarios: training from scratch versus continued pre-training of an existing pretrained model; cost estimates based on Chinchilla scaling laws, Kaplan FLOPs formula, and A100 80G GPU pricing', 'key_findings': 'EHR text data are likely insufficient for training very large LLMs from scratch at many institutions; for example, a 65B-parameter model would require about 4.4 TB of data and cost about $3.4M for one training run, while a GPT-3/ChatGPT-size model would require about 12.4 TB and cost about $25.6M. Continued pre-training on existing models is substantially cheaper and may be more feasible for institutions with limited data. The paper concludes that data scale, compute scale, and budget constraints should strongly shape institutional LLM strategy.', 'evaluation_metrics': 'Token-to-GB ratio; optimal training token size; dataset size; estimated FLOPs; estimated computing time; estimated training budget/cost', 'biomedical_task': 'Planning and feasibility analysis for training biomedical/clinical LLMs on electronic health record data; institutional decision support for model acquisition, from-scratch training, and continued pre-training', 'llm_model_or_family': 'ChatGPT; GPT-4; LLaMA (including LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-33B, LLaMA-65B); GPT-2; GPT-3; Chinchilla; BLOOM', 'biomedical_domain_context': 'Electronic health records; clinical informatics; healthcare institution AI deployment; inpatient and outpatient hospital notes', 'study_type': 'Methodological paper; analytical framework / cost and scaling analysis', 'comparison_baselines': 'Comparison across model sizes and training strategies rather than predictive baselines; contrasted training from scratch with continued pre-training; referenced LLaMA-65B, GPT-2, GPT-3/ChatGPT-size models as size/cost comparators', 'limitations_or_risks': 'The paper notes that EHR data are duplicative and unclean, and that data cleaning may change usable scale. It is an open question whether a model trained from scratch only on EHR data would be useful or whether general-domain text is necessary. The work does not quantify cloud versus on-premises trade-offs, and cost estimates exclude human resources, preprocessing, iteration time, and regular updates. It also highlights uncertainty about the right data ratio, number of training passes, and frequency of retraining.'}
